title: ZipClear
question: How does a zip work?
hook: Two rows of tiny teeth, each with a bump on top and a hollow underneath, and one slider with a wedge inside. See in slow motion how a zip locks tooth by tooth, why you cannot pull it apart sideways, and why a worn slider makes it split.

explainer.title: Two tapes, two rows of teeth, one slider
explainer.text: A zip is two cloth tapes, each with a row of small teeth clamped along a corded edge. The rows are offset by half a pitch, so every tooth faces a gap. A slider rides on both rows, and stops at the ends keep it on.

explainer.title: A bump on top, a hollow underneath
explainer.text: Each tooth head has a small bump on top and a matching hollow below. In a closed zip the heads are stacked like cups. To slide out sideways a tooth would have to climb over one bump and let go of another, and it has only a few hundredths of a millimetre of play.

explainer.title: The slider bends the tape
explainer.text: Inside the slider is a Y-shaped channel. It bends each tape with the teeth on the outside of the curve, so the heads fan apart for a moment. As the rows converge, each head tips into the open gap across the way, one tooth at a time. Then the channel runs straight and the gaps close.

explainer.title: A wedge, working on one tooth at a time
explainer.text: Going down, the diamond in the fork of the Y is a wedge driven between the rows. A pull along the zip becomes a push sideways: pull ÷ (2 × tan(φ + λ)). The closed chain can hold hundreds of newtons sideways, but the slider needs only a few, because it frees a single tooth at a time.

explainer.title: Why a zip splits behind the slider
explainer.text: A slider is cast from soft zinc alloy. When its channel spreads by a few tenths of a millimetre, it no longer presses each bump fully into its hollow, and a tug rides the teeth apart. Squeezing the slider gently with pliers closes the channel again.

explainer.title: Metal, moulded plastic and coil
explainer.text: Metal teeth are stamped and clamped on. Plastic teeth are moulded on to the tape. A coil zip is one long nylon spiral whose loops act as teeth, and it is the commonest of all. The size number, such as #5, is roughly the width of the closed chain in millimetres.

concepts.def: One of the small shaped pieces along the edge of a zip tape. Two rows of them lock together.
The distance from one tooth to the next on the same tape. The two rows are offset by half a pitch.
The moving part of a zip. Its Y-shaped channel meshes the teeth going one way and parts them going the other.
The wedge inside the top of the slider that drives between the two rows to open the zip.
Spare room for a part to move. Locked zip teeth have almost none, which is why they cannot climb over each other.
A simple machine: a slope that turns a push in one direction into a push at right angles to it.
The sideways pull a closed zip can take before it fails, tested on 25 mm of chain.
A zip whose teeth are the loops of one long plastic spiral sewn to the tape.
A slider with a sprung pin that drops between two teeth when you let go of the pull tab, so the zip stays put.
